questions.q: In which year did the Congress party lose its majority in the Lok Sabha for the first time, marking the end of the "Congress system" as defined by political scientists?
questions.a: 1989. The Congress won 197 seats (down from 415 in 1984) and lost its parliamentary majority. A wrong answer (e.g., 1977, 1996, or 2014) reveals confusion between the first non-Congress government (1977 Janata Party), the first stable coalition era (1996 United Front), or the return of single-party majority (2014 BJP). The 1989 election is the specific turning point where Congress remained the largest party but could not form a government alone.

questions.q: Why did the Congress party, despite being the single largest party in the 1989 Lok Sabha (197 seats), choose to sit in opposition rather than form a minority government?
questions.a: Congress lacked a majority (272 needed) and, crucially, had no natural allies willing to support it; the National Front (Janata Dal + regional parties) already had a pre-poll understanding and secured outside support from BJP and Left Front. A wrong answer (e.g., "Congress didn't want to rule" or "President didn't invite them") reveals misunderstanding of parliamentary government formation: the President invites the leader most likely to command a majority; Congress realised it couldn't cobble together 272 votes without ideological compromises it wasn't ready to make, so it opted for opposition.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "coalition government" to the 1989 National Front government: Was it a coalition government or a minority government supported by outside parties? Justify using the distinction between "joining the cabinet" and "outside support."
questions.a: It was a **minority government supported by outside parties**, not a coalition government. The National Front (Janata Dal + regional parties) formed the cabinet; BJP and Left Front provided "outside support" (voting confidence but not taking ministerial berths). A wrong answer calling it a "coalition government" reveals confusion between coalition (parties share cabinet portfolios) and minority government with outside support (parties support on floor but stay out of cabinet). This distinction matters for accountability and policy coherence.

questions.q: Analyse the ideological contradiction in the 1989 arrangement: BJP (right-wing, Hindutva) and Left Front (left-wing, Marxist) both supported the same National Front government. What does this reveal about the nature of coalition politics in India?
questions.a: It reveals that **coalition politics in India is often driven by negative consensus (keeping a common opponent out) rather than positive ideological agreement**. BJP and Left had diametrically opposed ideologies but shared a short-term goal: prevent Congress return. A wrong answer focusing on "ideological convergence" or "policy agreement" misses the pragmatic, power-sharing logic that defines Indian coalitions — parties align tactically, not ideologically.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The end of the Congress system weakened Indian democracy because coalition governments are inherently unstable and ineffective." Use evidence from 1989–2014 to support or refute.
questions.a: The statement is **refutable**. While coalitions (1989–2014) saw 11 governments in 25 years, they also passed landmark legislation (RTI Act 2005, MGNREGA 2005, Nuclear Deal 2008, GST Constitution Amendment 2016) and deepened federalism by empowering regional parties. Instability is a feature, not a fatal flaw; coalitions forced consensus-building and accommodated diversity better than the Congress system's "accommodation within one party." A wrong answer accepting the premise uncritically reveals a bias toward single-party majorities and ignores the democratic value of power-sharing in a plural society.

questions.q: Create a hypothetical scenario: It is 1996. The BJP emerges as the single largest party (161 seats) but cannot prove majority. As President, you must decide whom to invite to form government. Draft a 3-point reasoning you would record in your decision note, citing constitutional conventions and the 1989 precedent.
questions.a: A good answer includes: (1) **Convention**: Invite the leader of the single largest party/pre-poll alliance first (BJP/NDA). (2) **Precedent (1989)**: Congress (largest party) declined; President invited V.P. Singh (National Front) who demonstrated support via letters from BJP and Left. (3) **Floor test requirement**: Give the invitee a fixed time (e.g., 2 weeks) to prove majority on the floor of the House. A poor answer omits the 1989 precedent or suggests the President can pick based on personal preference, revealing ignorance of constitutional conventions and the role of the President as a constitutional head bound by precedent.
